section.title: Deliver Me from Evil Men
section.sectionRationale: A Davidic lament against violent, deceitful enemies, this psalm belongs to the cluster of individual laments, Psalms 140-143, that close out Book V before David's final blessing psalms, its confidence that the LORD upholds justice for the poor and needy grounding honest prayer against real, documented cruelty in trust rather than personal revenge.
section.thesis: Surrounded by violent men whose tongues are as sharp as serpents and whose traps are hidden along his path, David refuses to take justice into his own hands, instead crying out to the LORD as his shield in the day of battle and resting in the certainty that God upholds the cause of the afflicted and needy.
section.frameNote: Four movements marked by Selah: the cry for rescue from violent, deceitful men, verses 1-3; the plea for protection from hidden traps, verses 4-5; confident petition to God the deliverer, verses 6-8; and trust in God's justice for evildoers and for the needy, verses 9-13.

units.label: Rescue me from evil men
units.note: the cry for rescue from violent, deceitful men

verses.text: Rescue me, O LORD, from evil men. Protect me from men of violence,
who devise evil in their hearts and stir up war all day long.
They sharpen their tongues like snakes; the venom of vipers is on their lips. Selah

units.label: Protection from hidden traps
units.note: the plea against snares and nets

verses.text: Guard me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked. Keep me safe from men of violence who scheme to make me stumble.
The proud hide a {{pach|snare}} for me; the cords of their net are spread along the path, and lures are set out for me. Selah
I say to the LORD, "You are my God." Hear, O LORD, my cry for help.
O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, You shield my head in the day of battle.
Grant not, O LORD, the desires of the wicked; do not promote their evil plans, lest they be exalted. Selah
May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused.
May burning coals fall on them; may they be thrown into the fire, into the miry pits, never to rise again.
May no slanderer be established in the land; may calamity hunt down the man of violence.
I know that the LORD upholds {{mishpat|justice}} for the poor and defends the cause of the needy.
Surely the righteous will praise Your name; the upright will dwell in Your presence.

pach.gloss: A snare, trap, or net, the sort hunters spread along a game trail. David pictures the proud hiding such traps along his own path, language that reappears almost identically at the close of Psalm 141, showing the same danger pressing David through this cluster of laments.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the legal right due to someone. David's confidence rests not in his own strength but in his certainty that the LORD Himself upholds mishpat for the poor and needy, the ground of every prayer in this psalm for deliverance and vindication.

basic.context: David cries for rescue from violent men whose words are as deadly as a serpent's venom and who set hidden traps along his path, likely reflecting seasons such as Saul's pursuit or Absalom's rebellion when slander and ambush were constant threats.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a real, historical danger David faced and the imprecatory prayers he offered in response; it prescribes bringing violent, deceitful opposition honestly to God as refuge and judge rather than taking retribution into one's own hands.
basic.originalLanguages: The proud hide a pach, snare, along David's path, the same trap imagery repeated at the close of Psalm 141. David's confidence rests on his certainty that the LORD upholds mishpat, justice, for the poor and needy, the legal vindication he cannot secure for himself.
basic.typology: David's plea, You shield my head in the day of battle, verse 7, anticipates the full armor of God believers are called to put on for spiritual warfare, Ephesians 6:10-17, and his confidence that God upholds the afflicted anticipates Christ's own care for the poor and oppressed, Luke 4:18.
basic.christ: Paul quotes verse 3's description of venomous speech in Romans 3:13 to describe universal human sinfulness, showing that the violence and deceit David faced from without also lodges within every human heart, a condition only Christ's righteousness can address, Romans 3:21-26.
basic.god: God is shown as shield, deliverer, and righteous judge, one who guards the vulnerable from hidden traps, restrains the schemes of the proud, and can be trusted to uphold justice for the poor and needy even when human courts fail.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:13 quotes verse 3 to describe the deceitful, venomous speech common to fallen humanity. Ephesians 6:10-17 develops the psalm's shield and battle imagery into the full armor of God for spiritual warfare. Romans 12:19 forbids personal revenge and entrusts justice to God, the same posture David models here.
basic.oneStory: David's cry for rescue from violent, deceitful enemies and his confidence that God upholds justice for the poor and needy anticipate the New Testament's diagnosis of universal sin and its promise of a Deliverer who shields His people in every spiritual battle and will finally right every wrong.

context.literary:
Psalm 140 is a lament of the individual, and it keeps a tight, almost mathematical shape. It opens with two requests that name the danger, 'Rescue me' and 'Protect me,' verse 1, and it will return to two more, 'Guard me' and 'Keep me safe,' verse 4. Between them, verses 2 and 3 describe the enemies and verse 5 their trap. The enemy appears in three images in a row: a mind that plots, a tongue that bites, and a snare laid on the path. Each of the first two sections ends with the word Selah, a pause in the music or a signal to lift the voice, so the psalm is paced in blocks.

At verse 6 the tone changes from complaint to confession. 'I say to the LORD, You are my God' is the centre of the poem. The verses before it are about what the wicked are doing; the verses after it are about what God does. Verse 7 gives a title for God, 'the strength of my salvation,' and a memory of past protection, 'You shield my head in the day of battle.' The psalm then moves to petition against the wicked, verses 8 to 11, and ends in confidence in verses 12 and 13, where the language of prayer becomes the language of knowledge: 'I know that the LORD upholds justice.'

Several threads run through the poem. The first is the vocabulary of violence: 'men of violence' appears in verse 1 and again in verse 4, and the same phrase closes the curse in verse 11, bracketing the wicked in the beginning and end of the prayer. The second is the trap: snare, cords, net and lures in verse 5 are answered by the fire and pits of verse 10, as if the trapper becomes the one trapped. The third is the head. The psalmist's head is shielded in verse 7, and in verse 9 the heads of his enemies are covered with the trouble of their own lips. The covering of the head by God is set against the covering of the heads of the wicked with their own words.

The poem is also a sequence of a hidden danger revealed and then exposed: the tongue, the snare, then the coals. The closing contrast of verse 13 sets 'the righteous' and 'the upright' in the presence of God against the 'man of violence' who has been hunted down. That final line is quiet, not triumphant.
context.historical:
The title gives Psalm 140 to David, and the likeliest setting is the long years in which he was hunted by Saul and by the men who fed Saul's suspicions. First Samuel names the informers who told Saul where David was: Doeg the Edomite, who reported to Saul and later killed the priests of Nob, 1 Samuel 22:9-19, and the Ziphites, who betrayed his hiding place, 1 Samuel 23:19. Psalm 52, written over Doeg, speaks of a tongue 'like a sharpened razor' and a 'deceitful tongue,' Psalm 52:2-4, which is very close to the imagery here. David's later reign also knew plots, such as Absalom's, so a later setting is possible, but the language of lying in wait fits the earlier years best.

A courtier's world is the world of this psalm. In the ancient Near East, politics ran on whispers, accusations and ambushes, and a rival could be destroyed by slander before a sword was drawn. The 'man of the tongue' in verse 11, which the BSB renders 'slanderer,' belongs to that world of court intrigue. The 'poor' and 'needy' of verse 12 are not a separate class from the king: David describes himself in the same terms in Psalm 40:17 and Psalm 86:1. A man who has been stripped of his position and hunted in the wilderness has become poor in every way that counts.

The trap imagery was drawn from hunting. The fowler's net, the pit and the snare were part of daily life in Israel, and these pictures recur throughout the Psalter, Psalm 91:3 and Psalm 124:7. The point is that the enemy's attack is not open war but concealed danger. It was a world of hunting for prey, and the prey had no weapon but prayer.

The reference to burning coals and fire in verse 10 would have called to mind the fate of Sodom, Genesis 19:24, and the vision of divine judgment in Psalm 11:6, which is exactly the language of the LORD raining fiery coals on the wicked. Israel had a long memory of how God dealt with violence, beginning with the flood, which came because the earth was 'full of violence,' Genesis 6:11.
context.canonical:
Psalm 140 draws on the vocabulary of the first book of the Psalter and carries it forward into the final books. The enemy's tongue as a sharpened weapon is found in Psalm 64:3-5, the scheme to hide a trap in Psalm 57:6 and Psalm 35:7-8, and the trapper trapped in Psalm 7:15-16 and Psalm 9:15. The wisdom books say the same: he who digs a pit will fall into it, Proverbs 26:27, and the ambushers lie in wait for their own blood, Proverbs 1:18. This is a settled principle in Israel's moral world, that violence recoils on the one who plans it.

Paul quotes verse 3 in Romans 3:13, 'The venom of vipers is on their lips,' in a chain of Old Testament verses showing that all humanity, Jew and Gentile, is under sin. The BSB footnote to Psalm 140:3 notes that citation. What David said of his enemies, Paul uses to describe the human condition apart from grace, and the sting is that none of us is exempt from the tongue's poison, as James 3:5-8 also argues. Jesus uses the same image in calling the religious leaders a 'brood of vipers,' Matthew 3:7 and 23:33, and the Revelation names the old serpent behind it all, Revelation 12:9.

The picture of burning coals on the head in verse 10 recurs in Proverbs 25:21-22, where the same phrase is turned into a way of treating an enemy, feeding him, and Paul quotes it in Romans 12:20 as part of overcoming evil with good. The psalm's vengeance language and the apostle's mercy language use the same image, which suggests that for the New Testament the real fire is the conviction that kindness brings.

The final verses draw on the long theme of the God of the poor: Deuteronomy 10:18, Psalm 12:5, Psalm 146:7-9, and Isaiah 11:4, where the Messiah judges the poor with righteousness. Jesus announced His mission to the poor, Luke 4:18, and promised the kingdom to them, Luke 6:20. The cry for justice becomes the cry of the souls under the altar, Revelation 6:10, and Jesus' own parable of the persistent widow, Luke 18:7-8.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted to give the hunted a way to pray. The psalm does not ask the reader to imagine an easy world. It names the real threats, plots, slander, and hidden traps, and teaches that these can be carried to God in detail. Specific prayer, with the enemy's methods spelled out, is a sign of trust and not of paranoia.

He also meant to teach where security lies. He does not boast of his own wisdom or strength. He says, 'You are my God,' verse 6, and then recalls that God has shielded his head in battle. His case is made not on his innocence alone but on his relationship with the LORD, and the weight of the poem rests on the character of God as the defender of the poor.

A third purpose is moral. The prayer for the wicked, verses 8 to 11, is not simply anger. David asks God not to grant the desires of the wicked, 'lest they be exalted.' The risk he fears is that evil may prosper and be taken as proof that God does not care. He wants the first hearers to hold to the conviction of verse 12, that the LORD upholds justice, even when the evidence is hard to see.

Finally, he wanted Israel to end the psalm with the quiet certainty of verse 13: the righteous will praise God's name and dwell in His presence. The fear and rage of the earlier verses are not the last word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's situation and his prayers. It does not tell believers to expect that their enemies will be burned or that they should wish for it as a personal project. Verses 9 to 11 are prayers addressed to God, not instructions to act. The poet leaves the action to the LORD, who alone may judge, and that is the pattern the New Testament endorses when it says 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,' Romans 12:19.

What the psalm prescribes is a way of praying when under attack. Name the danger plainly. Ask for protection in specific terms. Confess God as your God. Remember how He has helped before. Ask that justice be done and that wickedness not prosper. End with confidence that the righteous will dwell in His presence. Those habits remain valuable.

Care is needed with the images of verse 10. 'Burning coals' and 'miry pits' are the language of poetry and of the LORD's own judgments, and they are not a model for how Christians should treat people. Jesus asks His followers to love enemies and pray for them, Luke 6:27-28. The right use of the imprecations today is to pray that evil will be undone, that the violent will be stopped, and that God's justice will come, and to let the final disposal of people be His. Paul shows how the same image of coals can become a call for kindness, Romans 12:20.

debates.question: How should believers pray the curses of verses 8 to 11?

views.label: As real prayers for justice that Christians may still pray
views.case: The prayers are addressed to God, not to the enemy, and they ask Him to do what only He can. The martyrs in Revelation 6:10 pray the same sort of prayer, 'How long, O Lord... until You avenge our blood.' On this view such prayers are right wherever oppression exists, and the church should not apologise for them.

views.label: As prayers against evil systems and powers more than against people
views.case: Paul says our struggle is 'not against flesh and blood' but against spiritual forces of evil, Ephesians 6:12. The violence, slander and snares are the work of a deeper enemy, and the prayer is that these will be thwarted. This keeps the psalm usable while protecting the command to love enemies.

views.label: As an Old Testament stage fulfilled and transformed in Christ
views.case: The coals of verse 10 reappear in Romans 12:20 as the effect of kindness on an enemy. Jesus bore the violence of men and prayed for those who did it, Luke 23:34. On this reading the psalm shows the honest cry of the oppressed and Christ shows its answer in mercy.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the prayer is entrusted to God rather than carried out by the one who prays. The best use today combines honesty about evil with the New Testament's command not to repay evil for evil.

debates.question: What is the 'fire' and 'miry pits' of verse 10?

views.label: Literal and final judgment
views.case: Fire and coals appear for the destruction of Sodom and in Psalm 11:6. The 'never to rise again' of the line suggests a final end, and many see the verse as a prayer for decisive judgment.

views.label: Poetic images of retribution in this life
views.case: Fire and pits are images, like the net and the snare, for the way evil returns on those who devise it. The phrase 'covered in the trouble their lips have caused' in verse 9 supports reading the fate as the consequence of their own speech.

debates.bearing: Either way, the poem presents the justice of God as fitting: the harm planned by the wicked becomes their own. The psalm does not say how or when, which leaves room for both a present and a final judgment.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm is full of the vocabulary of danger, and the word choices show how the poet saw it. In verse 1 'men of violence' translates ish chamasim, literally 'man of violences,' from chamas, the word that describes the earth before the flood, 'full of violence,' Genesis 6:11. Chamas is not mere roughness; it is violence that wrongs and tears at the weak, and it is the sin God cannot tolerate. The phrase comes back in verses 1, 4 and 11, so the psalm both opens and closes with the same name for the enemy.

In verse 2 they 'stir up war,' using a verb that means to gather or stir up, as if war were raised like a storm. They do it 'all day long,' so that the attack has no rest. The wicked 'devise evil in their hearts,' where heart is the seat of planning, and the evil they plan is called ra'ot, a plural meaning evils or calamities.

Verse 3 is the striking image: they 'sharpen their tongues like snakes.' The word for the venom is chemah, a term also used for burning wrath, and the viper is called akshub. This word for viper is found only here in the Old Testament, which is why Paul's quotation in Romans 3:13 draws attention. Paul uses the Greek word for an asp. The tongue is a weapon sharpened for striking, and the venom is hidden until it enters the wound. Selah, which closes the verse, is a word whose exact meaning is unknown. It may mark a musical pause or a lifting of the voice, and the psalm uses it three times, in verses 3, 5 and 8.

Verse 4 says the wicked 'scheme to make me stumble.' The verb means to push or thrust, and the object is 'my steps': they aim to knock him off the path. Then verse 5 names four trapping tools: pach (snare), chavalim (cords), resheth (net) and moqeshim (lures or traps). Two of them, pach and moqeshim, come together again in Psalm 141:9, so the two psalms are twins in their vocabulary of hunting.

Verse 7 calls God 'the strength of my salvation.' The word for 'strength' is oz, strength that shields, and 'salvation' is yeshuah, the word from which the name Yeshua or Jesus comes. The phrase 'shield my head' uses a verb of covering. In Hebrew the covering is the kind that a screen or helmet provides, and the verb in verse 9, for covering the heads of the wicked, is a different word, so the psalm plays on two kinds of covering, one protective and one punishing.

Verse 12 says the LORD 'upholds justice for the poor.' The word for justice is mishpat, and the poor is ani, one who is bowed down or afflicted, with evyon, the needy one who begs. The psalm closes with the two verbs 'praise' and 'dwell,' for the righteous will give thanks to God's name and sit in His presence, a settled seat which is more than visiting.

typology.type: The hunted righteous man ensnared by hidden plots, verses 4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: David, set upon by informers and ambushes, prefigures the greater Son of David who was watched and trapped. The Pharisees sent men to 'catch Him in His words,' Mark 12:13, and sought 'to catch Him in something He might say,' Luke 11:54. The escalation is that the trap finally closed in a night arrest and a mockery of a trial, Luke 22:63-65, and yet in it His enemies fulfilled the purposes of God. The type falls short in that David prayed to be spared the snare, while Jesus went through it for others and rose.

typology.type: The tongue like a viper, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Paul takes the psalm's picture of venomous lips as a description of the whole fallen human race, Romans 3:13, and Jesus calls the leaders a 'brood of vipers,' Matthew 23:33. The serpent of Genesis 3 is the deepest source of such speech, as Revelation 12:9 identifies the old serpent as the devil. The escalation lies in Christ who, 'when they heaped abuse on Him,' did not retaliate, 1 Peter 2:23. The type has a limit: David's enemies were particular men, whereas the New Testament teaches that this poison is in every human heart until it is healed.

typology.type: The LORD who defends the cause of the poor, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's confidence about the poor and needy becomes concrete in the ministry of Jesus. He read from Isaiah that He was sent 'to preach good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18, and said, 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God,' Luke 6:20. Mary rejoiced that the hungry were filled with good things, Luke 1:53. The escalation is that God does not only uphold the cause of the poor from heaven but became poor Himself, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The type is incomplete in the psalm because it expects justice but does not yet see the Defender arrive.

typology.type: Burning coals on the head of the enemy, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: The same picture is used by Solomon, Proverbs 25:21-22, and by Paul, Romans 12:20, as a way to overcome an enemy by feeding him. The psalm sees coals as judgment; the apostle sees them as the pain of conscience when kindness meets hostility. The escalation is the cross, where the greatest evil was met with the greatest good and where the word 'Father, forgive them' was spoken, Luke 23:34. The correspondence is of image and is not a claim that the psalm foresaw the cross; it falls short in that judgment and mercy are held apart in the psalm and joined only in Christ.

study.christ:
Psalm 140 is a prayer of a righteous sufferer, and the New Testament repeatedly shows Jesus living the pattern in full. There is no verse of this psalm that the Gospels apply to Him by name, so the links are those of theme, pattern and contrast, and the only direct New Testament use, Romans 3:13, is of sinners.

First, Jesus is the hunted Righteous One. David was pursued by men who lied to the king, and Jesus was shadowed from the beginning of His ministry. The leaders sent spies to catch Him in His words, Luke 20:20 and Mark 12:13, and when that failed they bribed an insider and made an arrest by night. Where David prays for rescue from men of violence, Jesus faces them with the words, 'this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness,' Luke 22:53. He prays in Gethsemane, as David does here, but He does not ask that His enemies be burned. Peter says of Him that He 'did not retaliate' and 'made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The cry to God for justice and the quiet entrusting of the whole matter to the Judge are the same act, and Jesus does it perfectly.

Second, Jesus is the defender of the poor. Verse 12 says the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy, and Jesus came to do just that. His first sermon applies Isaiah's words to Himself, Luke 4:18-19. He tells the poor that the kingdom is theirs, Luke 6:20, and He becomes poor so that others may be rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. Isaiah foresaw that the Messiah would judge the poor with righteousness and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips, Isaiah 11:4, and in the Gospel that is the way of the one who is the Word.

Third, Jesus defeats the serpent whose venom lies on the tongues of the wicked. The psalm's snakes speak of an old enemy. By His death He destroyed 'him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,' Hebrews 2:14, and the promise that God will 'soon crush Satan under your feet,' Romans 16:20, is worked out through Him. Where the psalm prays 'Guard me,' Christ is the one who guards His own and says none will be snatched from His hand, John 10:28.

Finally the psalm ends with the righteous dwelling in God's presence, verse 13. Jesus says He goes to prepare a place so that His people may be where He is, John 14:2-3, and in the new creation His servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The only way the righteous can have that place is by His righteousness being theirs, which the psalm leaves unspoken and the gospel supplies. The reader should not read the psalm as a prophecy of Calvary, but as the prayer of one of the types of Christ that He completes.
study.god:
Psalm 140 is a prayer under pressure, and what it shows of God is shaped by that pressure. It shows the God who is for the weak.

The psalm names Him as the personal God: 'You are my God,' verse 6. In the middle of a poem about violence the poet puts the covenant relationship, and he says it aloud. The prayer is not a flight to a distant deity but a claim on the God who has bound Himself to His people, and who has the right to be addressed that way. The same name is used throughout, the LORD, Yahweh, repeated in each section of the poem.

God is a strong deliverer. 'The strength of my salvation' tells us that salvation is not a matter of the poet's skill. The picture of God shielding his head in the day of battle belongs to the same imagery as God as shield in Psalm 3:3, and the psalmist can speak of past experience of God's help. A God who has shielded before can be trusted to shield again.

God is the judge of those who do evil. The prayer of verses 8 to 11 rests on the conviction that God's governance of the world includes setting wrongs right. He does not grant the desires of the wicked, and He can turn their plans against themselves. The psalm teaches that this is not the believer's work but God's, so a believer is freed from the need to take revenge.

God is the defender of the poor. Verse 12 rests on a fact the whole Bible affirms: He is the God who sides with the oppressed. Deuteronomy 10:18 says He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and Psalm 146:7-9 lists those He lifts. A God like that is not neutral in a conflict between the violent and the weak. This truth should shape the church's concern for the vulnerable.

The tension the psalm holds is between trust and visible danger. The snares are still laid, the tongues still sharp, and yet the poet says 'I know.' The knowledge is not based on sight but on the character of the One he addresses. The pattern of lament that ends in confidence, found throughout the Psalter, is how faith lives where evidence is mixed.

For worship the psalm teaches us to name our dangers honestly, to speak to God by name, and to leave judgment to Him. It gives the church words to pray for those under attack, and it ends where all true worship ends: in praise of the name of the LORD and a place in His presence.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes the line about the venom of vipers on the lips as one of a chain of texts showing that all people are under sin. A prayer about David's enemies becomes a mirror for the whole human race, and it shows why the gospel offers a righteousness that comes from God and not from ourselves.

Written about Doeg the Edomite, it speaks of a tongue like a sharpened razor and a deceitful tongue. It supplies a likely historical background for the imagery of sharpened tongues in Psalm 140:3, and shows that David knew from experience what slander could do.

The wicked man digs a pit and falls into it, and his violence falls on his own head. This is the principle behind Psalm 140:9-10, that the trouble planned for others comes back on its author. The two psalms share the picture of the head and of the trap that turns.

Keep me from the snares they have laid for me, and from the lures of evildoers. The next psalm uses the same pair of words, snare and lure, as Psalm 140:5. The two prayers are close companions and may be read as a double petition against the same danger.

If your enemy is hungry, give him food, for you will heap burning coals on his head. It takes the image of coals in Psalm 140:10 and turns it from judgment into a way of overcoming an enemy by kindness.

Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves, but to leave room for God's wrath, and to overcome evil with good. It shows how the prayers against enemies in Psalm 140:8-11 should be handled in the church: handed to God, with kindness as the believer's own conduct.

The earth was corrupt and full of violence. The word for violence is the one in Psalm 140:1, 4 and 11, so that the psalm's 'men of violence' belong to the long line of those whose violence calls for God's judgment, going back to the days before the flood.

The LORD executes justice for the oppressed, sets prisoners free, lifts those weighed down and sustains the fatherless and widow. It spells out in detail the God Psalm 140:12 describes as the defender of the needy, and sets that work within a hymn of praise.

Jesus announces that the Spirit has anointed Him to preach good news to the poor. It is the Messiah's own commitment to the people whose cause Psalm 140:12 says the LORD defends, and it shows that the confidence of the psalm finds its answer in His ministry.

Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces of evil. It lets the believer read the enemies of Psalm 140 as human agents of a deeper opposition, and it explains why the armour of Ephesians 6:16-17 includes a shield and a helmet, as the psalm speaks of a shielded head.

The martyrs under the altar cry out, asking how long until their blood is avenged. They pray in the tradition of Psalm 140:8-11, appealing to God's justice, and they are told to wait. It shows how the church may take up the psalm's prayers while leaving the timing with God.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 140 belongs to a story that begins with a serpent. In Genesis 3 the tempter came with a question and a lie, and the curse on him set his offspring against the woman's offspring, Genesis 3:15. The 'venom of vipers' in verse 3 and the plots against the righteous are the continuing front of that war. From the murder of Abel, Genesis 4:8, to the violence that filled the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11, the first chapters of the Bible show what it looks like when the serpent's seed lives by lies and force.

God's answer in the Old Testament is to raise up a people whose King is the defender of the poor. The law protects the fatherless and the widow, Deuteronomy 10:18. The prophets rebuke rulers who devour the needy. The Psalms put the cry of the oppressed into the mouth of the righteous, and Psalm 140 is one of its sharpest examples. David is hunted, but he is also the anointed king, so his prayer carries the hope that the line of promise will be preserved.

The psalm looks ahead to Christ, the Son of David, who is hunted by the same kind of enemies, who trusts the Father with His life, and whose death and resurrection break the power of the serpent. After His victory, the church takes up these prayers, and the New Testament shapes how they are prayed: with love of enemies, patience for God's timing, and confidence in His justice. The cry of the martyrs in Revelation 6:10 is the same cry, now offered under the altar of the Lamb.

The end of the story is that the dragon, 'that ancient serpent,' is thrown down, Revelation 12:9, and finally removed, Revelation 20:10. The poor and needy are no longer waiting for an advocate: the one on the throne dwells among them, and 'He will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:3-4. The last line of the psalm, that the upright will dwell in God's presence, becomes the closing promise of the Bible, that His servants will see His face and His name will be on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4. The prayer of a hunted man in a cave becomes the song of a people who are safe at last.

quiz.q: How does David describe the words of the violent men opposing him in verse 3?

options.text: Their tongues are sharpened like snakes, with the venom of vipers on their lips.
options.note: This vivid image of deadly, deceitful speech is quoted by Paul in Romans 3:13.

options.text: Their words are harmless but their actions are dangerous.
options.note: The verse specifically targets their speech itself as venomous and deadly, not merely their actions.

options.text: Their words are confused and lack any real threat.
options.note: The imagery is of sharp, deliberate, deadly speech, not confusion.

options.text: Their words are honest but harsh in tone.
options.note: The venom imagery signals deceitful, destructive speech, not simply blunt honesty.

quiz.q: What have the proud done according to verse 5?

options.text: Hidden a snare and spread cords of a net along the path David walks, with lures set out for him.
options.note: This hunting imagery pictures deliberate, hidden schemes designed to trap David unaware.

options.text: Openly declared war on David in a public battle.
options.note: The imagery is of hidden, secret traps, not open, declared warfare.

options.text: Offered David a peace treaty he refused to sign.
options.note: The verse describes concealed danger, not any offer of peace.

options.text: Built a wall to keep David out of the city.
options.note: The image is of snares and nets along a path, not a defensive wall.

quiz.q: What confession does David make in verse 6?

options.text: "You are my God," a direct declaration of trust and allegiance to the LORD amid danger.
options.note: This simple, personal confession anchors the psalm's confident petition that follows.

options.text: That he no longer trusts God to help him.
options.note: The confession is one of trust, the opposite of despair or doubt.

options.text: That he will handle the situation using his own military strength alone.
options.note: The verse turns to God for help rather than relying on self-sufficiency.

options.text: That his enemies are actually more powerful than God.
options.note: The confession affirms God's supremacy and calls on Him as deliverer, not the reverse.

quiz.q: What does David know for certain about the LORD, according to verse 12?

options.text: That the LORD upholds justice for the poor and defends the cause of the needy.
options.note: This settled confidence in God's justice grounds the whole psalm's trust rather than despair.

options.text: That the LORD only helps kings and never the poor.
options.note: The verse specifically affirms God's care for the poor and needy, not only the powerful.

options.text: That justice in this life is impossible to find.
options.note: The verse expresses confident certainty that God does uphold justice, not hopelessness about it.

options.text: That David himself must personally punish every wrongdoer.
options.note: The verse credits the LORD, not David's own hand, with upholding justice.

quiz.q: What does David expect for the righteous, according to verse 13?

options.text: That the righteous will praise God's name and the upright will dwell in His presence.
options.note: This closing confidence turns the lament toward worship and future fellowship with God.

options.text: That the righteous will suffer forever with no relief.
options.note: The verse expects the opposite, praise and dwelling in God's presence for the upright.

options.text: That the righteous will eventually become just as violent as their enemies.
options.note: The psalm contrasts the righteous with violent men throughout, not equates them.

options.text: That only David alone, and no one else, will be vindicated.
options.note: The verse speaks broadly of the righteous and the upright, not David exclusively.

questions: David names his enemies' venomous speech directly to God rather than retaliating in kind. What deceitful or hurtful words are you facing right now, and what would it look like to bring them honestly to God instead of responding in kind?
Hidden snares were set along David's own path. Where do you sense hidden temptation or danger along your path this week, and how can you ask God to guard you from it?
David's confession, You are my God, anchors his whole prayer. What would change in your current situation if you began there, simply reaffirming whose you are, before asking for anything else?
David entrusts judgment of his enemies to God rather than acting himself. Is there a situation where you are tempted to take justice into your own hands rather than trusting God's timing?

David is certain the LORD upholds justice for the poor and needy even when he cannot see it happening yet. Where do you need that same certainty today, in a situation where justice still seems delayed?

translationNotes.note: Paul quotes this verse directly in Romans 3:13 as part of his catalog of Old Testament texts proving universal human sinfulness, the venom of asps under their lips.

May the heads of those who surround me be covered in the trouble their lips have caused reflects a common psalm pattern in which the evildoer's own scheme becomes the very trouble that falls back upon them.
Justice renders the Hebrew mishpat, a legal term for the right verdict or vindication due to someone, here confidently attributed to the LORD's ongoing care for the poor and needy.
